title: Web crawler: many slow fetches in flight, a seen set in memory
brief: Design a web crawler, e.g. one that fetches 1 billion pages a month for a search index. A scheduler decides which URLs are due (seeds, newly found links, pages due for a re-crawl) and hands them to the URL frontier; fetchers download each page; a parser pulls out its links and content; page bodies go to blob storage. In the sim the client block is that scheduler: it releases URLs at the crawl rate, and each URL counts as a write (it ends in a stored page). A real frontier holds billions of URLs waiting their turn; the sim's queue holds only the ones released and not yet fetched, so its backlog means the fetchers are falling behind the crawl rate. Remote sites are slow: a fetch takes hundreds of ms to seconds (this lesson uses 1 s, an estimate). Model a fetcher replica as a worker holding 100 connections open: capacity 100 pages/s, base latency 1000 ms. The sim does not derive capacity from latency: you set capacity = connections ÷ fetch time yourself (Little's law).

requirements: 770 pages/s at peak: 1B pages / 30 days ≈ 386/s on average, ×2 for peak

~100 KB of HTML per page (an estimate); page bodies go to blob storage. The sim counts requests, not bytes, so it can't see why a month of pages doesn't belong in a SQL database: that argument is yours
A fetcher replica holds 100 connections, 1 s per fetch: a worker with capacity 100, base latency 1000 ms
handing a URL to the frontier: p99 < 200 ms (the scheduler never waits for a fetch)
cost < $1.35/hr (the sim's generic worker costs $0.10/hr, less than a real fetch box, so this budget is about how many fetchers you run, not real dollars)
Link extraction and the seen-URL check are the freshness variant's topic: here each fetched page is one write to blob storage
variants.twist: Many sites slow down: the average fetch doubles to 2 s. A fetcher with 100 connections now finishes 50 pages/s, but the sim won't lower capacity on its own: set the fetchers to capacity 50, base latency 2000 ms and watch the backlog. Get back under budget: more fetchers, more connections per fetcher (with async I/O one box can hold many more), or a shorter fetch timeout that gives up on the slowest sites? Which of those loses pages? (The sim has no fetch timeout of that kind: talk that one through.)

requirements: Re-crawl news: 30,000 hub pages (homepages and section fronts), each re-fetched every 2 minutes: 250 fetches/s
Each hub page has ~150 links (an estimate), and every link is checked against the seen-URL set. Almost all are already known; only new articles get queued
Mark the fetchers' edge into the seen set as fan-out on write (the lesson sets followers = 150): one fetched page becomes 150 lookups. The sim counts each lookup as a write
The sim has no Bloom filter block: any store block can stand in for the seen set. It also has no loops, so the few new links that would go back into the frontier aren't modeled
Same fetcher as the broad crawl: worker, capacity 100, base latency 1000 ms
handing a URL to the frontier: p99 < 200 ms
variants.twist: Politeness: one publisher has 3,000 of the 30,000 hub pages, so every 2 minutes means 25 requests/s to one host. Its robots.txt asks for at most one request per second (e.g. a Crawl-delay line, a non-standard directive some crawlers honor). How often can each of its pages be re-fetched now, which of its pages get the slots, and how do you hold that host back without stalling every other site's fetches? (The sim has no per-host limits: talk it through.)

hints: If one fetch takes a second, how many have to be in flight to finish 770 a second, and should the scheduler wait for any of them? Freshness: for each hub page you fetch, how many seen-set lookups happen?

Put a queue (the frontier) between the scheduler and the fetchers, and size the fetchers by pages in flight: in flight = rate × fetch time. The seen-set check runs once per link, not once per page, so it needs a store that answers tens of thousands of lookups a second cheaply; a set of known URLs this size fits in memory.

Broad: scheduler -> service -> queue -> fetchers (capacity 100, latency 1000) -> blob, with enough fetchers to stay below full utilization. Freshness: the same pipeline plus a fan-out-on-write edge from the fetchers to the seen set; price a KV store sized for 37,500 lookups/s against one in-memory store (a cache block, or e.g. Redis).
_notes: Fetcher = worker, capacity 100, base 1000 ms: 100 servers per replica (c = capacity x latency), so it barely queues until it's nearly full. Broad: 770 writes/s. Inline (scheduler -> service -> 10 fetchers -> blob): default timeouts give over 90% errors (the 1 s service timeout vs 1 s fetches, then client retries pile on); 60 s timeouts still give p99 over 1 s. Queued (service -> queue -> fetchers -> blob): 7 fetchers fall behind (backlog 8,400 after 120 s); 8 (rho 0.96) pass, $1.10; 9: $1.20; 10: $1.30; 11 ($1.40) break the budget. Page bodies in SQL instead of blob fail only on cost here ($1.55 with 8 fetchers); the real reason is the byte volume, which the sim doesn't count. Twist: capacity 50 at 2000 ms: 15 fetchers fall behind; 16 keep up but cost $1.90; 8 fetchers at capacity 100 and 2000 ms (200 connections each) pass at $1.10. Freshness: 250 fetches/s x 150 links = 37,500 lookups/s on the fan-out edge. client -> service -> SQL with the fan-out: over 90% errors. Seen set in SQL (5k/s) falls behind; KV with 3 replicas (30k/s) falls behind; KV 4 (rho 0.94) keeps up but costs $1.80. Cache block as the seen set (50k/s, rho 0.75): 2 fetchers fall behind (backlog 6,000 after 120 s); 3 fetchers (rho 0.83) pass, $0.75; 4: $0.85; 5: $0.95; 6 ($1.05) break the budget. Redis instead of the cache block with 3 fetchers: $0.82. Without the fan-out edge the fan-out check fails. Grade beyond the sim: (1) Interfaces: frontier enqueue(url, priority) and dequeue() -> a URL whose host may be hit now; fetcher: resolve DNS (cached, since one host serves many pages), check robots.txt (fetched and cached per host), HTTP GET with a timeout and a size cap; parser: extract links and text; store: page body to blob storage, metadata to a KV or wide-column store; new links: normalize (lowercase host, drop fragments, resolve relative paths), check the seen set, enqueue the new ones. (2) Data model: URL record keyed by a hash of the normalized URL: url, host, last fetched at, HTTP status, content hash, next fetch at, priority. Seen set of URL hashes: a Bloom filter can give false positives (a new URL looks seen and is skipped, so a page is missed) but never false negatives (a seen URL never looks new, so no duplicate crawls); about 10 bits per URL gives 1% false positives (textbook Bloom filter math, not a sim number). Content hash of the body catches exact duplicates (mirrors, the same page under several URLs); near-duplicates need a similarity hash such as SimHash or MinHash. (3) Trade-offs: politeness vs throughput: a per-host limit caps how fast one site can be crawled, so throughput comes from many hosts in parallel; usual answer is per-host queues (e.g. Mercator-style front queues for priority, back queues per host with a next-allowed time). BFS vs priority: plain BFS from seeds is simple but spends the budget on whatever is near the seeds and can sink into crawler traps (endless calendar pages, session IDs in URLs); priority by importance or by how often a page changes spends fetches better. Freshness vs coverage: re-crawls compete with new pages for the same fetchers; conditional GET (If-Modified-Since, or If-None-Match with the page's ETag, answered with 304 Not Modified) makes unchanged re-crawls cheap. Bloom filter vs exact set: memory vs missed pages. Checked in frontend/src/lessons/content.test.ts. Real-world source: Najork & Heydon, 'High-Performance Web Crawling' (Mercator, Compaq SRC Research Report 173, 2001): k front FIFO queues by priority, n back queues each holding one host, and a heap of when each host may next be contacted; politeness waits 10x the last download time from that host; about 3x as many back queues as fetch threads. Its seen-URL set is exact: 8-byte fingerprints (about 5 GB for 1B URLs, or a disk-based merge), not a Bloom filter. Both are fair answers; the exact set never skips a page.
